quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this 'turn up' means arriving, not increasing volume.
quests.hint: This means arriving somewhere, often unexpectedly or after being absent.
quests.explanation: 'Turn up' can also mean to arrive somewhere, often unexpectedly, a completely different meaning from the 'increase volume' sense you already know. The pattern of missed meetings is the clue pointing to arrival here.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically turns — the phrase describes someone appearing after a period of absence or uncertainty.
quests.contextSentence: After missing the last three meetings, he finally turned ___ this morning.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — a very casual, informal way to describe arriving.
quests.hint: This means arriving somewhere in a very casual, relaxed way, often late.
quests.explanation: 'Roll up' is a very informal, casual way to describe arriving somewhere, often suggesting a relaxed, unbothered attitude, sometimes about being late.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, borrowing the casual image of someone strolling in nonchalantly, as if rolling into a scene.
quests.contextSentence: He just rolled ___ twenty minutes late, like it was no big deal.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that fits the meaning in this context — this is a formal document, so register matters here.
quests.hint: This means arriving, expressed in a plain, neutral way suitable for formal writing.
quests.explanation: 'Shown up' is neutral and appropriate for formal writing, unlike 'rolled up,' which sounds far too casual for an official incident report. 'Turned up' would also be understood, but 'shown up' is the safest, most standard choice in formal registers.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase simply describes someone's unexpected arrival, expressed here in neutral, professional language.
quests.contextSentence: In his formal incident report, the security guard wrote that an unauthorized visitor had ___ at the loading dock without identification.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — a very casual way to describe quitting something for good.
quests.hint: This means quitting or stopping something completely, in a very casual, conversational tone.
quests.explanation: 'Pack it in' means to quit or stop doing something for good, often a job or routine, expressed in a relaxed, informal way rarely used in professional writing.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, borrowing the image of packing your things away for the last time before leaving something behind entirely.
quests.contextSentence: After thirty years, she decided to pack it ___ and retire to the countryside.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that fits the meaning in this context — this is a formal resignation letter, so register matters here.
quests.hint: This means resigning from a position, expressed in language suitable for a formal letter.
quests.explanation: 'Step down' is the standard, formal choice for a resignation letter, unlike 'pack it in,' which would sound jarringly casual in that context. 'Give up' is too vague and general for describing leaving a specific position.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase compares leaving a position of authority to descending from a higher level, expressed here in formal language.
quests.contextSentence: In her formal resignation letter, she explained that she wished to ___ from her position as director.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This means never quitting, expressed in the same casual tone as earlier in this level.
quests.explanation: This reinforces 'pack it in,' describing a stubborn refusal to ever fully retire, in the same relaxed, conversational register introduced earlier in this level.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes stopping an activity completely, expressed in casual, everyday language.
quests.contextSentence: My grandad always said he'd never pack it ___ , even at eighty-five.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — a common, softer way to describe someone losing their job.
quests.hint: This means dismissing someone from their job, often used as a softer, more formal alternative to 'fired.'
quests.explanation: 'Let go' is a common, somewhat euphemistic way to describe an employee being dismissed, often for reasons like budget cuts rather than personal fault.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physical is released — the phrase softens the harshness of dismissal into gentler, more formal language.
quests.contextSentence: Due to budget cuts, twenty employees were let ___ last month.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this reviews a phrase about disappointing someone.
quests.hint: This means disappointing someone by failing to follow through on a promise.
quests.explanation: This reviews 'let down,' meaning to disappoint someone, distinct from 'let go' (dismiss from a job) and 'let off' (excuse from punishment) — all part of the same LET family with very different meanings.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase compares disappointing someone to letting them fall after relying on your support.
quests.contextSentence: After promising to help, I really didn't want to let her ___ by canceling at the last minute.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this means excusing someone from a deserved punishment.
quests.hint: This means excusing someone from a punishment they might otherwise have received.
quests.explanation: 'Let off' means to excuse someone from punishment, often with a lighter consequence than expected, such as a warning instead of a fine. It completes a small family alongside 'let go' and 'let down.'
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically released — the phrase describes a punishment being reduced or waived.
quests.contextSentence: The judge decided to let him ___ with just a warning, given it was a first offense.

quests.instruction: Select the correct phrase to complete the sentence.
quests.hint: This means finally telling the full truth after a period of lying.
quests.explanation: 'Come clean (about something)' means to finally admit the full truth, especially after a period of dishonesty or hiding something significant.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, borrowing the image of washing away the dirt of dishonesty by finally telling the whole truth.
quests.contextSentence: After weeks of lying, he finally decided to come ___ about what really happened.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that fits the meaning in this context — this suits a dramatic confession after extended, serious deception, not a single small mistake.
quests.hint: This means confessing fully after a long period of serious, hidden deception.
quests.explanation: 'Came clean' fits a dramatic, full confession after months of serious secret deception. 'Owned up' would suit admitting one specific, smaller mistake, and doesn't carry the same sense of finally revealing a long-hidden truth.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes finally revealing a truth that had been deliberately hidden for a long time.
quests.contextSentence: After months of secretly gambling away the family savings, he finally sat everyone down and ___.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This means an organization finally admitting to something it had concealed for a long time.
quests.explanation: This reinforces 'come clean,' showing that the phrase applies to organizations as well as individuals, especially after years of concealing a serious problem.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes finally admitting a truth that had been hidden for a long time.
quests.contextSentence: The company was pressured to come ___ about the safety issues it had been hiding for years.

quests.instruction: Choose the option with the correct word order for this separable phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This reviews 'take off' with a pronoun object — remember, pronouns must sit between the verb and the particle.
quests.explanation: 'Take off' is separable, so with a pronoun object like 'it,' the particle must follow the pronoun: 'take it off,' never 'take off it.' This word-order rule applies to many two-word phrasal verbs you've already learned.
quests.literalVsFigurative: This question tests grammar rather than meaning — 'take off' still means removing clothing; only the pronoun's position is being tested.
quests.contextSentence: It's warm in here — why don't you ___?

quests.instruction: Choose the option with the correct word order for this non-separable phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This reviews 'look after' with a pronoun object — unlike separable verbs, this particle never moves.
quests.explanation: 'Look after' is non-separable, meaning the particle 'after' always stays right next to 'look,' with the object — pronoun or noun — following afterward: 'look after him,' never 'look him after.'
quests.literalVsFigurative: This question tests grammar rather than meaning — 'look after' still means taking care of someone; only the correct fixed word order is being tested.
quests.contextSentence: The dog needs feeding twice a day — can you ___ while we're away?

quests.instruction: Choose the option with the correct word order for this separable phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This reviews 'sort out' with a pronoun object — remember the separable word-order pattern from earlier questions.
quests.explanation: 'Sort out' is separable, so with a pronoun object like 'it,' the particle follows the pronoun: 'sort it out,' never 'sort out it.' This is the same pattern you saw with 'take it off.'
quests.literalVsFigurative: This question tests grammar rather than meaning — 'sort out' still means resolving a problem; only the pronoun's position is being tested.
quests.contextSentence: There's a problem with the invoice — I'll ___ tomorrow.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this 'break down' means separating something into parts for clarity.
quests.hint: This means dividing something, like a cost or a report, into smaller, clearer parts.
quests.explanation: 'Break down (something)' can mean to divide it into smaller, clearer components, such as splitting a total cost into categories. This is a transitive use — it takes a direct object — different from the intransitive uses you've already learned, like a machine breaking down on its own.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically splits apart — the phrase describes organizing information into clearer, smaller components.
quests.contextSentence: Can you break ___ the total cost into separate categories for the report?

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this uses the same 'itemize' sense from earlier in this level.
quests.hint: This means dividing an annual figure into smaller, more manageable time periods.
quests.explanation: This reinforces the transitive, 'itemize' sense of 'break down,' here applied to splitting an annual budget into monthly figures for easier review.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes organizing a large figure into smaller, clearer parts.
quests.contextSentence: The finance team carefully broke ___ the annual budget into monthly figures so it would be easier to review.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this is the intransitive sense you already know, describing equipment failure.
quests.hint: This means a machine failing on its own, without anyone deliberately doing anything to it.
quests.explanation: This contrasts with the transitive sense earlier in this level — here, 'broke down' is intransitive, describing the projector failing on its own, with no direct object involved.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: the projector genuinely stops functioning, unrelated to the figurative 'itemize' sense taught earlier in this level.
quests.contextSentence: Right in the middle of the presentation, the projector suddenly broke ___, leaving everyone in the dark.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this 'set out' means presenting ideas in a document, not beginning a journey.
quests.hint: This means clearly presenting or stating something, such as objectives in a written proposal.
quests.explanation: 'Set out' can also mean to clearly present information in a structured way, especially in writing, a different sense from 'begin a journey,' which you learned much earlier in this curriculum.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically arranged — the phrase describes organizing ideas clearly within a document.
quests.contextSentence: The proposal sets ___ three clear objectives for the coming year.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb.
quests.hint: This means clearly presenting expectations or a plan to other people.
quests.explanation: 'Lay out (something)' means to clearly present a plan, set of expectations, or set of options to others, often at the start of a project or meeting.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, borrowing the image of laying items out on a table so everyone can see them clearly at once.
quests.contextSentence: The manager laid ___ her expectations for the project at the very first meeting.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that fits the meaning in this context — this needs the most explicit, unambiguous option of the three.
quests.hint: This means stating something with total, explicit clarity, leaving nothing vague or open to interpretation.
quests.explanation: 'Spell out' fits explicit, unambiguous detail, matching 'rather than leaving things vague.' 'Lay out' would suit presenting a general plan, and 'set out' fits formal written statements — neither implies quite the same total clarity as 'spell out.'
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes explaining something so explicitly that no ambiguity remains.
quests.contextSentence: The CEO decided to spell ___ exactly which targets needed to be hit by December, rather than leaving things vague.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this involves formal, legal paperwork.
quests.hint: This means formally transferring legal ownership of something through a signed document.
quests.explanation: 'Sign over (something)' means to formally transfer legal ownership, typically through a signed legal document, such as property passing to a family member.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal in the sense that a real signature is genuinely required to complete the legal transfer.
quests.contextSentence: He signed the house ___ to his daughter before he passed away.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — this describes giving up control or responsibility, without necessarily involving legal paperwork.
quests.hint: This means transferring control or responsibility to someone else, in a general sense.
quests.explanation: 'Hand over (something)' means to transfer control or responsibility to someone else, more broadly than 'sign over,' which specifically implies a formal legal document.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is always physically passed by hand — the phrase describes transferring responsibility or authority to someone else.
quests.contextSentence: The outgoing president handed ___ power to his successor in a peaceful ceremony.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that fits the meaning in this context — this involves no legal paperwork at all, unlike a more formal transfer.
quests.hint: This means informally transferring day-to-day responsibility, without any legal contract involved.
quests.explanation: 'Handed over' fits an informal transfer of responsibility, confirmed by 'without any legal paperwork.' 'Signed over' would specifically require a legal contract, which the sentence explicitly rules out.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes an informal transfer of responsibility between two people.
quests.contextSentence: Because there was no formal contract involved, the founder simply handed ___ day-to-day control to his business partner, without any legal paperwork.

quests.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — a casual, everyday way to decline something.
quests.hint: This means casually declining something offered to you, in a relaxed, informal tone.
quests.explanation: 'Pass on (something)' means to casually decline an offer, often used in relaxed, everyday conversation rather than formal writing.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically passed to anyone — the phrase describes declining an offer in a light, casual way.
quests.contextSentence: Thanks for the invite, but I think I'll pass ___ the party this time.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that fits the meaning in this context — this is a formal email, so register matters here.
quests.hint: This means declining an offer, in language appropriate for formal written communication.
quests.explanation: 'Turn down' is the more standard, neutral choice for formal written communication, unlike 'pass on,' which feels noticeably more casual and spoken, less suited to an official email.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes declining an offer, expressed here in more formal, professional language.
quests.contextSentence: In her formal email declining the invitation, she wrote that she would have to ___ the generous offer due to a scheduling conflict.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — the same casual register from earlier in this level.
quests.hint: This means casually declining something because you're too tired, in a relaxed, spoken tone.
quests.explanation: This reinforces 'pass on' in the same casual, spoken register as earlier in this level, here declining an evening plan due to tiredness.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes a light, casual decision to decline something.
quests.contextSentence: I'm exhausted, so I think I'll pass ___ drinks tonight.

quests.instruction: Choose the correct particle to complete the phrasal verb — a review of the LET family from earlier in this file.
quests.hint: This means excusing someone from a deserved punishment with a lighter consequence instead.
quests.explanation: This revisits the LET family from earlier in this file. 'Let off' fits excusing someone from a deserved punishment, distinct from 'let down' (disappoint) and 'let go' (dismiss from a job).
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes a punishment being reduced or waived rather than fully enforced.
quests.contextSentence: Even though company policy would have justified serious punishment, the manager decided to let the intern ___ with just a verbal warning.

quests.instruction: Choose the phrase that fits the meaning in this context — a review of the transfer-of-control pair from earlier in this file.
quests.hint: This means an informal transfer between neighbors, without any legal document involved.
quests.explanation: This revisits SIGN OVER vs HAND OVER from earlier in this file. The casual, informal nature of the exchange — 'without any written agreement' — clearly points to 'handed over' rather than the legally formal 'signed over.'
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative, as before — the phrase describes an informal transfer of an object between two people who trust each other.
quests.contextSentence: Since it was just a friendly favor between neighbors rather than a real business transaction, she simply handed ___ the extra key without any written agreement.

quests.instruction: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence — a fitting idiom for speaking honestly and directly, closing this stage of register-focused learning.
quests.hint: This means speaking plainly and directly about something, without softening it with polite or vague language.
quests.explanation: 'Call a spade a spade' means to speak plainly and directly about something, without euphemism or avoidance. It's a fitting idiom to close this file, which has explored so many shades of formal, informal, casual, and direct language.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Fully figurative: no actual spades are involved — the phrase compares calling something by its honest, plain name to naming a simple tool exactly what it is.
quests.contextSentence: Rather than dancing around the issue with polite language, the new director prefers to call ___ and address problems head-on.
